title: Two axes of a new Middle East
gist: A new Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement' and an informal India-Israel-UAE 'Indo-Abrahamic' alignment are emerging as two competing axes binding Middle East security to the Indian subcontinent, though Shinde cautions the blocs are not cleanly opposed and the US remains the decisive, unpredictable variable.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the 'Mecca Joint Defence Agreement' on 7 August 2026, under which an attack on any one of the three Sunni Muslim states is to be treated as an attack on all three.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Marks a formal new Sunni-Muslim mutual-defense bloc that reshapes Middle East security architecture and signals reduced reliance on US guarantees.
insights.locator: A Pakistan-Saudi-Turkey defence pact

insights.claim: Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the Mecca pact contains 'no common threat that we have put in writing' and that its NATO Article 5-like mutual defense clause would depend on the 'circumstances,' signaling a deliberately ambiguous commitment.
insights.speaker: Hakan Fidan
insights.so_what: The hedged wording suggests the pact is more a political signal than a binding military commitment, limiting how much investors should price it as a hard security guarantee.
insights.quote: There is no common threat that we have put in writing
insights.locator: opening quote from Hakan Fidan

insights.claim: Shinde interprets the Mecca pact primarily as a signal to Washington that Gulf states like Saudi Arabia are prepared to handle their own defense against Iran, given what Riyadh sees as the US's 'lackadaisical attitude' toward protecting their sovereignty from Iranian attacks.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Signals Gulf states hedging away from reliance on US security guarantees, a factor relevant to oil-market risk premia and regional defense spending.
insights.quote: lackadaisical attitude to protecting their sovereignty against Iranian attacks
insights.locator: In the last few months, Gulf capitals

insights.claim: The Mecca pact follows a bilateral Saudi-Pakistan mutual defense agreement signed the previous September, shortly after Israel killed Hamas leaders in Doha.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Shows the trilateral pact builds on an existing bilateral security relationship rather than emerging from nowhere.
insights.locator: Notably, last September, Riyadh and Islamabad

insights.claim: The Mecca pact functions for Turkey as a shield against regional rival Israel, whose recent strikes on Tehran unnerved Turkish defense circles despite not toppling the Islamic Republic.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Explains Turkey's motive for aligning with Gulf Sunni states as balancing against Israeli military capability, not primarily an anti-Iran move.
insights.locator: While it may not have brought down

insights.claim: Erdoğan and Netanyahu have an openly hostile personal relationship, with Erdoğan calling Netanyahu 'a relative of Hitler' and Netanyahu labelling Erdoğan a dictator, reflecting a rivalry that runs deeper than personal animus.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Illustrates that Turkey-Israel tension is a structural feature of the region, likely to persist and shape alignment choices for years.
insights.locator: In the past, Erdoğan has used

insights.claim: Erdoğan has framed Turkey's regional ambitions in explicitly historical-imperial terms, invoking Ottoman military victories from Badr to Manzikert to Gallipoli at the reopening of the Hagia Sophia mosque.
insights.speaker: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan
insights.so_what: Signals Turkey's ambitions extend beyond immediate security needs toward a self-conception as a resurgent regional-imperial power.
insights.quote: The resurrection of the Hagia Sophia represents our memory full of heydays in our history from Badr to Manzikert, from Nicopolis to Gallipoli.
insights.locator: In a speech to mark the opening of the Hagia Sophia mosque

insights.claim: Turkey and Pakistan share an ideological affinity through mutual support for political Islam, including the Muslim Brotherhood and Hamas, distinguishing them from more secular Gulf states like the UAE and Oman.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Explains why Turkey-Pakistan cooperation runs deeper and longer than transactional security ties, complicating the Mecca pact's cohesion with more secular Saudi interests.
insights.locator: In the politico-cultural realm

insights.claim: Turkey has been expanding its military and naval reach toward the Indian Ocean, building a naval base in Somalia and exploring the use of Pakistani ports, a move Shinde says could turn Turkey into an 'Indo-Pacific player.'
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Points to Turkey's naval expansion as a longer-term strategic shift worth tracking for shipping-lane and Indian Ocean security implications.
insights.locator: At the same time, it has built a naval base in Somalia

insights.claim: For Pakistan, the Mecca pact offers a way to project international status and responsibility despite a 'tottering economy and a turbulent domestic situation.'
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Suggests Pakistan's participation is driven as much by domestic legitimacy needs as by genuine military strategy.
insights.quote: tottering economy and a turbulent domestic situation
insights.locator: Like Turkey, Pakistan also benefits

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have deep Cold War-era defense ties, including thousands of Pakistani military personnel who served as engineers, aviators, and trainers in Saudi Arabia, and Saudi financial support for Pakistan's nuclear infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Establishes that the Mecca pact formalizes a decades-old institutional relationship rather than a new alignment.
insights.locator: During the Cold War, thousands of Pakistani officials

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia and Turkey historically competed for leadership of the Sunni Muslim world -- including the 1920s Saudi conquest of Mecca and Medina from the Hashemites -- and clashed publicly over the 2018 murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi in Istanbul, but shared concern over Iran and Israel has since driven them together.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Shows the Mecca pact represents a genuine reversal of a historically adversarial relationship, making it more strategically significant than a routine alliance.
insights.locator: Historically, the House of Saud rose up

insights.claim: Shinde notes Middle Eastern security pacts have a poor survival record, citing the 1979 dissolution of the Baghdad Pact and the ongoing fragmentation of the Gulf Cooperation Council as reasons for skepticism about the Mecca agreement's durability.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations that the new pact will prove a lasting structural shift rather than a short-term hedge.
insights.quote: spaghettis of security cooperation that have perished in bureaucratic files
insights.locator: To be sure, Middle Eastern states have a varied history

themes.theme: The Indo-Abrahamic axis: India, Israel, UAE

insights.claim: Egyptian-American analyst Mohammed Soliman labels the informal India-Israel-UAE grouping the 'Indo-Abrahamic' coalition in his book West Asia, and argues the US indirectly backs it while China tacitly approves of the Pakistan-Turkey-Saudi nexus.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Frames the two Middle East axes as loosely proxying a broader US-China great-power competition, relevant to investors tracking bloc-based realignment.
insights.locator: In his new book West Asia

insights.claim: The UAE normalized relations with Israel via the 2020 US-brokered Abraham Accords, and ties have held steady through Israel's Gaza and South Lebanon campaigns, with Israel even deploying its Iron Dome and Iron Beam defense systems on Emirati soil during the Iran conflict.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the depth of UAE-Israel security integration, a relationship that would have been unthinkable a decade ago and now anchors the informal Indo-Abrahamic axis.
insights.quote: Deploying such technology on Arab soil, even a decade ago, would have been called ludicrous.
insights.locator: In the ongoing Iran conflict

insights.claim: India-Israel ties shifted from a covert, low-profile relationship to an open partnership after Narendra Modi's 2017 visit, the first by a sitting Indian prime minister, now spanning counter-terrorism, critical technology, and arms sharing.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Marks a clear inflection point in 2017 after which India-Israel defense and technology cooperation became a strategic pillar rather than a discreet backchannel.
insights.quote: Prime Minister, we’ve been waiting for you a long time, 70 years in fact.
insights.locator: When Narendra Modi became the first Indian prime minister

insights.claim: Minilateral groupings such as I2U2 (India-Israel-UAE-United States) and the India-Cyprus-Greece-Israel alignment notably exclude both Turkey and Iran, whose political elites define themselves in opposition to Israel.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Shows the institutional architecture of the Indo-Abrahamic camp is deliberately structured to exclude the Mecca-pact bloc's key members.
insights.locator: Minilateral groups like the India-Israel-UAE-United States

themes.theme: The UAE's moderation as a strategic asset

insights.claim: Unlike Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 push, the UAE has built its brand around religious moderation and toleration, opposing radical political Islam across Yemen, Egypt, Qatar, and Pakistan, a stance Shinde says is rooted in institutional memory of Cold War-era Arab nationalism, not just technocratic calculation.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Explains why the UAE, despite being Muslim-majority, has become a natural partner for Israel and India rather than aligning with the Turkey-Pakistan bloc.
insights.locator: The stupendous growth of Dubai and Abu Dhabi

insights.claim: Shinde cautions against treating the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan axis and the India-Israel-UAE axis as cleanly opposed blocs, noting Saudi Arabia maintains strong economic and political ties with India despite its historic support for Pakistan and new alignment with Turkey.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Warns against over-simplified bloc analysis when assessing regional risk, since key players like Saudi Arabia straddle both camps.
insights.locator: For one, Delhi has reasonable relations with Riyadh

insights.claim: Before the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack, Saudi Arabia was moving toward normalizing relations with Israel, a process that Israel's subsequent actions in Gaza have since stalled.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Shows Saudi-Israel normalization remains a live but currently frozen possibility that could reshape both axes if revived.
insights.locator: Before 7 October 2023, Riyadh was also cosying up to Israel

insights.claim: Shinde argues the US remains the single most important and unpredictable variable in the region: despite deepening ties with the UAE and India, Israel still has no substitute for direct American security backing.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers should treat the two-axis framing as secondary to US policy decisions, which remain the primary swing factor for regional stability.
insights.quote: Israel’s trustworthy partnerships with the UAE and India are additional safeguards but not direct substitutes for concrete and committed American support.
insights.locator: Perhaps the most important uncertainty, however, remains the position of the United States

insights.claim: Shinde frames both the Mecca agreement and the informal Indo-Abrahamic axis as evidence of a historic British-era concept of 'Southwest Asia,' in which Middle Eastern and Indian subcontinental security have become inseparable.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Suggests analysts should stop treating Middle East and South Asia security as separate theatres, since both new axes now directly link the two regions.
insights.quote: the winds of the Middle East have reached the floodplains of the Indian subcontinent.
